rewritten_text:
My father's surname was Pirrip and my given name Philip, but as a small child I could manage nothing longer or clearer than Pip when trying to say them together. So I called myself Pip, and Pip became the name everyone used.

I know that my father's surname was Pirrip from his gravestone and from my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. I never saw either of my parents, or even a picture of them, since they lived long before the time of photographs. My earliest ideas of their appearance therefore came, quite irrationally, from their gravestones. Something about the lettering on my father's made me imagine a broad, solidly built, dark man with curly black hair. From the style and curves of the inscription, “Also Georgiana Wife of the Above,” I reached the childish conclusion that my mother was freckled and sickly. Beside their grave stood a neat row of five little diamond-shaped stones, each about eighteen inches long, commemorating my five little brothers, who had abandoned the universal struggle to make a living remarkably early. These stones gave me a belief I held with absolute faith: that all five had been born lying on their backs with their hands in their trouser pockets, and had never taken them out for the whole of their earthly existence.

We lived in the marsh country beside the river, less than twenty miles from the sea along the river's winding course. My first vivid, wide-reaching sense of what things actually were seems to have come on one memorable, bitter afternoon as evening approached. I discovered then, with certainty, that this desolate, nettle-covered place was the churchyard; that Philip Pirrip, formerly of this parish, and Georgiana, wife of the above, were dead and buried; and that Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, their infant children, were also dead and buried. The dark, flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, crossed by ditches, banks, and gates, with cattle scattered over it grazing, was the marshes. The low, lead-gray line beyond was the river, and the distant wild lair from which the wind came rushing was the sea. And the small, shivering bundle that was growing frightened of everything and beginning to cry was Pip.

“Stop that noise!” shouted a terrifying voice, as a man sprang up among the graves beside the church porch. “Keep quiet, you little devil, or I'll cut your throat!”

A frightening man, dressed entirely in coarse gray clothes, with a heavy iron shackle on his leg.

I don't want any part of business like that, I says to myself.

When I come downstairs next morning, the parlor was closed and the people who'd been watching was gone. Nobody was about except the family, widow Bartley, and our lot. I kept looking at their faces to find out if anything had happened, but I couldn't make nothing of it.

Along about noon the undertaker arrived with his helper. They put the coffin on two chairs in the middle of the room, then arranged all our other chairs in rows and fetched more from the neighbors, till the hall, parlor, and dining-room was full up. I noticed the coffin lid was just as it had been, but with people standing around I didn't dare try peeking underneath.

Then folks started pouring in, and the frauds and the girls sat in the front row by the coffin's head. For half an hour people passed slowly round in single file and gazed at the dead man's face for a minute, and some let a tear fall. Everything was quiet and solemn, except for the girls and the frauds keeping their heads down and their handkerchiefs at their eyes and giving a little sob now and again. You couldn't hear anything else but feet scraping over the floor and noses getting blowed, because folks always blows their noses more at funerals than anywhere else, barring church.

Once the rooms was crammed, the undertaker slipped about in his black gloves, all soft and soothing, attending to the finishing touches and settling people and things comfortable and orderly. He didn't make any more noise than a cat. Never a word from him; he shifted folks about, wedged in the late arrivals, and cleared passages, all by nodding and waving his hands. Then he stationed himself against the wall. I never saw a man so quiet and gliding and sneaky in his movements, and he hadn't any more smile about him than a ham.

They'd borrowed a melodeum, and it was an ailing one. When all was ready a young woman sat down to play it, and it squealed and groaned something awful. Everybody joined in the singing, and to my thinking Peter was the only one getting the best of the bargain. Then Reverend Hobson started speaking, slow and grave; and right that minute the most tremendous racket you ever heard broke out down in the cellar. There was just one dog, but the noise he made was powerful, and he went on and on without letting up. The parson had to stand over the coffin waiting, because you couldn't so much as hear yourself think.

For an instant astonishment prevented me from thinking clearly. I knew that my drawing differed greatly from this in its particulars, though the general outlines bore a certain resemblance. At length I fetched a candle, sat down at the far end of the room, and began to examine the parchment with greater care. Turning it over, I discovered my own sketch on the reverse, precisely as I had drawn it. My first response was simple wonder at the extraordinary likeness of the outlines: at the strange coincidence that a skull should, without my knowledge, have occupied the other side of the parchment directly beneath my representation of the scarabæus, and that it should correspond so nearly with my drawing in both shape and dimensions. The oddness of this coincidence, I repeat, left me wholly bewildered for a while. Such coincidences commonly have this effect. The mind labours to discover a connection, some chain of cause and consequence, and when it fails, falls into a kind of momentary paralysis. Once this bewilderment passed, however, a conviction gradually took hold that startled me much more than the coincidence itself. I began to recall, clearly and unmistakably, that no drawing had been on the parchment when I sketched the scarabæus. Of this I became entirely sure, remembering that I had examined first one side and then the other to find the cleanest place. Had the skull been present, I could not possibly have overlooked it. Here was a mystery that seemed beyond explanation. Yet even then, in the farthest and most hidden recesses of my understanding, there appeared to flicker a faint, glow-worm gleam of the truth so splendidly established by last night's adventure. I stood up immediately, secured the parchment in a safe place, and postponed further thought until I could be alone.

“After your departure, and when Jupiter was sound asleep, I commenced a more orderly examination of the matter. I first reflected upon the circumstances through which the parchment had reached my hands. We had found the scarabæus on the mainland shore, roughly a mile east of the island and only a little above the high-water line. When I seized the insect, it bit me sharply, making me drop it. Jupiter, displaying his usual prudence, looked around for a leaf or some similar object before attempting to grasp the creature, which had flown in his direction. He intended to use this to take hold of it.”
